title: In Defense of the Unitary Scalarization for Deep Multi-Task Learning
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
problem_statement: Investigating whether complex, specialized multi-task optimization (SMTO) algorithms consistently outperform simple unitary linear scalarization (equal weighting) when baselines are properly tuned.
domain: Deep Multi-Task Learning, Multi-Objective Optimization, and Computational Efficiency
theoretical_framework: Linear Scalarization vs. Specialized Multi-Task Optimization (SMTO), Pareto Optimality, and Regularization Theory
methodology: Rigorous benchmarking comparing unitary scalarization against specialized MTO algorithms (MGDA, GradNorm, PCGrad, CAGrad, IMTL) across computer vision, reinforcement learning, and NLP benchmarks using standardized hyperparameter tuning protocols.
evaluation: Per-task performance metrics, relative multi-task transfer, training runtime in wall-clock seconds, and peak GPU memory allocation.
key_findings: Demonstrated that unitary scalarization (equal weighting) combined with standard modern optimization techniques (Adam, learning rate warmup, weight decay) matches or exceeds the performance of complex SMTO methods.
Showed that specialized MTO algorithms introduce massive computational overhead, running 2x to 35x slower than simple scalarization due to multiple backward passes.
Concluded that many SMTO algorithms function primarily as implicit regularizers rather than superior optimization engines.
scope_and_delimitations: Evaluates hard-parameter-sharing architectures across vision and reinforcement learning benchmarks under controlled hyperparameter budgets.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: Our experiments focus on benchmarks where tasks are moderately related. In scenarios with extreme task imbalance or severely conflicting gradients, specialized loss weighting may still offer advantages.
limitations.summary: Acknowledged that scenarios with extreme task gradient scale disparities or severe negative transfer may still benefit from adaptive optimization.

generalizability_gap: Does not evaluate low-resource code-switched NLP tasks (such as Taglish disaster triage) or heterogeneous token-versus-sequence loss landscapes.
methodological_gap: Did not decouple intra-task sample gradient variance from inter-task gradient conflict.
future_work: Investigating low-overhead adaptive loss weighting methods that retain the computational efficiency of scalarization while preventing gradient scale dominance.
